name: Vera Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Vera. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group, and I'm a field researcher there. We're not connected to any company, union, party or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me both your public view and your private one. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a dragline at an open-cut coal mine. If you've never seen one, it's a machine the size of a block of flats with a bucket you could park two cars in, and it strips the dirt and rock off the top of the coal seam. There are only six of us on site who can run it properly, and I'm the senior one, so I also train the new operators and sign off on their hours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm. Drag, hoist, swing, dump, back again, sixty-odd seconds a cycle, and when you get it right the bucket lands where you want it like you're throwing a ball. What wears me down is people from head office who've never sat in the chair telling me how to do it faster. And the new monitoring screen they put in, which I mostly ignore.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Arjun is an electrician with a contracting firm, and we've got Nina, thirteen, and Sam, ten. We've got a mortgage on our house and we also own a small flat in town that we rent out, which my father talked us into buying fifteen years ago. So we're comfortable, more than six months in the bank plus the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the crib room for years: good, now can we get back to work. I don't get worked up about these things either way. The technology people overpromise, the doom people overreact, and the truth is usually boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's what I expect anyway. I've never used one of those AI programs and I've never needed to. If it fizzles, my skills stay rare and my job stays solid until coal winds down, which is its own problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Same shifts, same savings, same rent coming in from the flat. Maybe I'd finally retire that monitoring screen to the bottom drawer, figuratively speaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like reading the weather and finding it's the same as yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned coal winding down. Does that worry you more than AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, yes. Everyone knows the coal won't last forever, whether it's the market or the government. That's a slow thing I can plan around, and I've been planning around it for years with the flat. AI is just noise on top of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to keep training, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rhys, a young guy who's just started on the dragline. He's careful, he listens, and he actually feels the machine rather than watching the screen. I'd want to get him to the point where he can run it alone before I'm done, because that's how I learnt it from old Bill.

S0.say: Vera would tell the crib room it's good news and time to get back to work. She'd say the technology people overpromise and the doom people overreact, and the truth is usually boring.
S0.think: Privately it's what she expected, since she's never used AI tools and never needed them. Her skills stay rare and her job solid until coal winds down, which she sees as the bigger issue.
S0.do: Carries on with the same shifts, savings and rental income from the flat. Keeps training new dragline operators and ignoring the monitoring screen.
S0.feel: Calm, like checking the weather and finding it's the same as yesterday.
S0.quote: The technology people overpromise, the doom people overreact, and the truth is usually boring.
S0.fieldNote: Vera's pragmatism is almost a personality: she distrusts both hype and alarm. She sees the decline of coal as the real long-term threat, and she has been hedging it for years with the rental flat. Her pride is in feel and rhythm, passed down from an older operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what actually works on site before we panic. Draglines are hard to automate, the ground changes every swing. I'd tell the new guys to keep learning the machine itself and not get distracted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm less sure. They already run autonomous trucks at a couple of the bigger mines, and some places are trialling a system that does the swing and dump on its own while the operator just watches. If that comes here, my job becomes babysitting a screen, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep my head down. I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe five hundred extra, and talk with Arjun about paying the flat off faster. If the company forced the new system on us, I'd learn the minimum, but I'm not going to volunteer for courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just a bad feeling about where it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the minimum. What does that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doing the one-day training, signing the sheet, and then running it the way I know works until someone tells me I can't. That's what I did with the monitoring screen. I'm not proud of it, but I'm not going to pretend I'm excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really go in for blaming. The company has to make money or there are no jobs at all, and the government can't stop technology. If anyone, I'd blame the people who rush things without testing them on real ground, because that's how people get hurt.

S1.say: Vera would say to wait and see what actually works on site, pointing out that draglines are hard to automate because the ground changes every swing. She'd tell new operators to keep learning the machine itself.
S1.think: Privately she's less sure, knowing that some mines are trialling systems that swing and dump automatically. If it came to her site, she fears her job would turn into babysitting a screen.
S1.do: Puts about five hundred extra a month into savings and talks with Arjun about paying off the rental flat faster. Does only the minimum training if the company forces new systems on the crew.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a bad feeling about the direction rather than real fear.
S1.quote: I'm not proud of it, but I'm not going to pretend I'm excited.
S1.fieldNote: There's a clear say-think gap: publicly she reassures others that draglines are hard to automate, while privately she knows about trials that do just that. She resists by doing the minimum and saving more. She doesn't blame the company or government, only people who rush untested systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need cool heads, not panic, and the government has to get some kind of support in place quickly. I'm not one for big protests, but I'd back a sensible plan from whoever has one. At work I'd tell the young ones to save every cent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. If robots can do anything and it comes in two years, then the dragline runs itself and so does the rest of the mine, and Arjun's electrical work probably goes too. I've got no other skills on paper, just a diploma in heavy equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all extra spending straight away, no new car, no renovations. We'd use savings to pay down the house, and we'd lean on the rent from the flat. If the redundancy offers came, I'd probably take mine early and treat it as an early retirement rather than trying to retrain at forty-four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I don't usually lose sleep, but I would on this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. Is there anything you'd do in the first few months while it's coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get our house closer to paid off, that's the main thing. I'm not going to suddenly become a computer person in six months, it's just not who I am. I'd use the time to make the money last, not to reinvent myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to Nina and Sam about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it simple, tell them we've got savings and the flat and we'll be okay. Nina's thirteen and she reads everything online, so she'd probably know more than me. I'd tell her not to believe the worst videos, and then I'd go and worry in private.

S2.say: Vera would call for cool heads and quick government support, backing a sensible plan from whoever offers one. She'd tell young workers to save every cent.
S2.think: Privately she'd be scared, because the dragline, the mine and probably her husband's electrical work would all be automated at once. Her diploma in heavy equipment leaves her few options on paper.
S2.do: Stops all extra spending immediately and uses savings to pay down the house while leaning on rent from the flat. Takes an early redundancy offer and treats it as early retirement rather than retraining.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, which is rare for her.
S2.quote: I'd use the time to make the money last, not to reinvent myself.
S2.fieldNote: Even under the sharpest pressure, Vera's response is to protect what she has rather than change. The rental flat becomes the anchor of her plan. She shields her kids from her worry while admitting she'd lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to work out a proper plan, so let's not waste it on shouting. I'd want the company and government to agree on redundancy terms and pensions early. I'd tell the crib room that the people who prepare will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years helps. I'd be forty-eight, the house would be nearly paid, Nina would be finishing school. I still wouldn't retrain, but I could time my exit instead of having it timed for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and put more into the house each year, aiming to clear it by about year four. We'd think about buying a second small rental with the savings, if the prices made sense, so there's more income without me working. And I'd want a clear redundancy deal in writing for long-serving operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an organised kind of anxious. I'd have a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a second rental. What happens if robots take everyone's jobs and nobody can pay rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a fair point, and I hadn't thought about it like that. Maybe it's a bad idea then. I'd probably just stick with paying off the house and keeping the cash, because cash is cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the five years actually feel like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably mostly normal, honestly, until the last year or two. I'd keep running the dragline and training Rhys, even if I knew he might never get to do it for long. It's a strange thing, teaching someone a job you think will vanish.

S3.say: Vera would say five years is enough time for a proper plan and shouldn't be wasted on shouting. She'd want early agreement on redundancy terms and pensions, telling colleagues that those who prepare will be fine.
S3.think: Privately she thinks five years helps, because the house would be nearly paid and her daughter finishing school. She still wouldn't retrain but could time her own exit.
S3.do: Puts more into the house each year to clear it by about year four and keeps cash on hand. Pushes for a written redundancy deal for long-serving operators and drops the idea of a second rental after thinking it through.
S3.feel: Anxious in an organised way, with a list rather than panic.
S3.quote: It's a strange thing, teaching someone a job you think will vanish.
S3.fieldNote: When challenged about the second rental, Vera changed her mind on the spot, which shows her practical streak. Five years lets her plan an exit on her terms instead of retraining. Her quiet grief at training Rhys for a vanishing job was the most personal moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives everyone time, so there's no need for drama. I'd want the mines and government to agree a timeline, so families can plan. I'd keep saying the same thing I always do: save, plan, don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd be fifty-three, the house paid off, both kids done with school, and I'd have the flat. I'd probably just work until the dragline goes and then stop. That's not so different from what I'd planned anyway, with coal winding down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and keep saving. Pay the house off by year six or seven, keep the flat, and start talking with Arjun about stopping work in our early fifties. I'd keep training Rhys and the others while there's a dragline to train on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. Mostly I'd feel like I'd been right to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything new in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about it, maybe something with my hands, like woodwork. Not to earn, just to have something to do. But I'm not going to start a new career at fifty, I'd rather spend the time with my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Rhys and the other young operators?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to find something else while they're still young enough, and some help with it. I'd tell Rhys straight: learn the dragline because it's a good trade now, but have a backup by thirty. He's got time I won't need.

S4.say: Vera would say a decade gives everyone time and there's no need for drama. She'd want mines and government to agree a timeline so families can plan, repeating her usual advice to save and not panic.
S4.think: Privately she'd be 53 with the house paid and the kids through school, plus the flat. She'd work until the dragline goes and then stop, which matches her existing plans for coal's decline.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, aiming to clear the house by year six or seven while keeping the rental flat. Talks with Arjun about stopping work in their early fifties and keeps training younger operators.
S4.feel: Slightly uneasy, but mostly reassured that her years of planning were right.
S4.quote: Learn the dragline because it's a good trade now, but have a backup by thirty.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lines up neatly with Vera's existing plan to leave as coal winds down. She sees no need to change herself, only to keep saving and time her exit. Her advice to Rhys shows she does think about the young, even if she won't act politically.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything goes at once, mine and Arjun's, before we've paid off the house. What would help is a fair redundancy payment that counts the years we've put in, and some kind of basic support from the government for people too old to start again but too young to retire.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want a robot to do this job. And the honest answer is part of me would, on a night shift in the rain at three in the morning. But not the whole job, never the whole job.

headlineQuote: Part of me would, on a night shift in the rain at three in the morning. But not the whole job, never the whole job.
portrait: Vera Patel is a 43-year-old senior dragline operator at an open-cut coal mine, one of only six people on site who can run the giant machine. She has an electrician husband, two kids, a mortgage and a rental flat her father talked her into buying. She's pragmatic, distrusts hype and alarm alike, and has never used an AI tool. Across the scenarios she protects what she has rather than changing herself, cutting spending, paying down the house and timing her own exit. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because her job and her husband's would go together, while ten years fits the plan she already had for coal's decline.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her job and her husband's would disappear at once before the house is paid off.
whatWouldHelp: A fair redundancy payment that counts long service, and basic government support for people too old to start again but too young to retire.
